email.scenario: You run a monthly repair gathering in your neighborhood, where volunteers help residents fix broken household items. The bookings coordinator at the municipal hall, Ms. Okafor, has offered you the hall for a Saturday next month. However, you have just learned that road resurfacing work will close the street outside the hall that day, so people could not bring heavy items to the door.

Propose holding the gathering on the following Saturday instead.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: This week we have been looking at old industrial districts where factories closed decades ago. Many of these buildings now have heritage status, and many of the surrounding neighborhoods face a housing shortage. Some cities allow such factories to be converted into apartments, while others insist that the original brickwork and machinery be kept exactly as built. What do you think? Should heritage factory buildings be converted into housing rather than kept in their original form? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Mateo
studentPosts.post: I think conversion is the better choice. A protected factory that stands empty helps nobody, and upkeep is expensive. If people live there, the building is heated, repaired and cared for. Families near old industrial districts need homes now, and the outside walls can still remind everyone what the place used to be.

studentPosts.name: Ingrid
studentPosts.post: I disagree. Once you cut a factory floor into apartments, the machinery goes and the interior no longer shows how people actually worked there. Brick walls alone are just decoration. Housing can be built on empty land nearby, but an original factory, once altered, can never be put back the way it was.
